questions.stem: A matrix has 3 rows and 2 columns. Its order is:
questions.explanation: The order is written as rows × columns, so 3 rows and 2 columns gives 3 × 2. A 2 × 3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns.

questions.stem: A symmetric matrix is a square matrix that:
options: has non-zero elements only on its leading diagonal
is equal to its own transpose
has only zeros below its leading diagonal
has every element equal to 1
questions.explanation: In a symmetric matrix the element in row i, column j equals the element in row j, column i, so swapping rows and columns changes nothing. Zeros below the diagonal describe an upper triangular matrix.

questions.stem: An identity matrix is a square matrix with:
options: exactly one 1 in each row, in any position
1s on the leading diagonal and 0s everywhere else
1s in every position of the matrix
0s on the leading diagonal and 1s everywhere else
questions.explanation: The identity matrix I has 1s down the leading diagonal and 0s elsewhere, and AI = IA = A. A matrix with exactly one 1 in each row and column, in any position, is a permutation matrix.

questions.stem: A square matrix has an inverse if and only if:
options: its determinant is equal to zero
it is a symmetric matrix
all of its elements are positive
its determinant is not zero
questions.explanation: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix involves dividing by the determinant, so it exists only when the determinant is non-zero. Many non-symmetric matrices have inverses.

questions.stem: A permutation matrix is a square binary matrix with:
options: a 1 in every position on the leading diagonal
at least one 1 in each row of the matrix
equal numbers of 1s and 0s in the matrix
exactly one 1 in each row and each column
questions.explanation: A permutation matrix has a single 1 in every row and every column and 0s elsewhere, so multiplying by it reorders rows or columns. The identity is one example, but not the only one.

questions.stem: For the product AB of two matrices to be defined:
options: A and B must both be square matrices of the same order
the number of rows of A must equal the number of columns of B
the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B
the number of rows of A must equal the number of rows of B
questions.explanation: Each element of AB pairs a row of A with a column of B, so they must have the same length. Matrices of different orders, such as 2 × 3 and 3 × 4, can still be multiplied.

questions.stem: In a transition matrix where each column is a current state and each row is the next state, each column adds to:
options: the number of states
questions.explanation: Each column lists where everything in one state goes next, so its proportions must account for the whole state and add to 1 (100%).

questions.stem: A transition matrix T is regular if:
options: T is a symmetric matrix
T is equal to its own inverse
some power of T has only positive elements
every column of T contains at least one 0
questions.explanation: A regular transition matrix has a power with no zero elements, and regular matrices lead to an equilibrium state. A matrix whose powers always keep a zero element is not regular.

questions.stem: In a Leslie matrix for a population divided into age groups, the top row contains:
options: the birth rates of each age group
the survival rates of each age group
the number in each age group
the death rates of each age group
questions.explanation: The top row of a Leslie matrix gives the average number of offspring per individual in each age group. The survival rates sit just below the leading diagonal.

questions.stem: In a communication matrix, an element of 1 in row A, column B means that:
options: B can send a message directly to A
A can send a message directly to B
A can send a message to B through one other person
A and B cannot communicate at all
questions.explanation: A one-step communication matrix records direct links from the row person to the column person. Two-step links, through one other person, are counted by the square of the matrix.

questions.stem: A matrix with zeros below the leading diagonal and any values on or above it is:
options: lower triangular
diagonal
symmetric
upper triangular
questions.explanation: Zeros below the leading diagonal leave the non-zero values in the upper triangle, so it is upper triangular. A diagonal matrix has zeros both above and below the diagonal.

questions.stem: The equilibrium (steady) state of a transition model is recognised when:
options: successive state matrices show no noticeable change
every element of the state matrix equals zero
the state matrix becomes the identity matrix
the transition matrix becomes a zero matrix
questions.explanation: For a regular transition matrix, repeated steps settle down so that S(n + 1) is essentially the same as S(n). The transition matrix itself never changes.

questions.stem: Matrix A has order 2 × 3 and matrix B has order 3 × 4. The order of AB is:
questions.explanation: The inner dimensions (3 and 3) match, so AB exists, and its order comes from the outer dimensions: 2 × 4. BA is not defined, because B has 4 columns and A has 2 rows.

questions.stem: The determinant of the matrix [4 3; 2 5] (rows separated by semicolons) is:
questions.explanation: For [a b; c d] the determinant is ad − bc = 4 × 5 − 3 × 2 = 20 − 6 = 14. Adding the products gives 26.

questions.stem: The inverse of the matrix [3 1; 5 2] (rows separated by semicolons) is:
questions.explanation: The determinant is 3 × 2 − 1 × 5 = 1. Swap the leading diagonal, negate the other two elements and divide by 1: [2 −1; −5 3]. Forgetting to swap the diagonal gives [3 −1; −5 2].

questions.stem: The matrix [k 4; 3 6] (rows separated by semicolons) has no inverse when k equals:
questions.explanation: No inverse exists when the determinant is zero: 6k − 4 × 3 = 0, so 6k = 12 and k = 2. k = 4.5 sets 4k − 18 = 0, using the wrong diagonal.

questions.stem: A 2 × 2 matrix A has elements given by the rule a(i, j) = 2i − j, where i is the row and j is the column. Matrix A is:
questions.explanation: a(1, 1) = 1, a(1, 2) = 0, a(2, 1) = 3 and a(2, 2) = 2, so the rows are 1 0 and 3 2. Swapping i and j gives the transpose, [1 3; 0 2].

questions.stem: The product [1 2; 3 0] × [2; 1] (rows separated by semicolons) is:
questions.explanation: Row 1: 1 × 2 + 2 × 1 = 4. Row 2: 3 × 2 + 0 × 1 = 6. A 2 × 2 matrix times a 2 × 1 matrix gives a 2 × 1 column matrix, not a row matrix.

questions.stem: A = [3 1; 0 2] and B = [1 4; 2 1] (rows separated by semicolons). The matrix 2A − B is:
questions.explanation: 2A = [6 2; 0 4], and subtracting B element by element gives [6 − 1  2 − 4; 0 − 2  4 − 1] = [5 −2; −2 3]. [7 6; 2 5] adds B instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: For A = [1 1; 0 1] (rows separated by semicolons), the matrix A² is:
questions.explanation: A² = A × A: row 1 gives 1 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 1 and 1 × 1 + 1 × 1 = 2; row 2 gives 0 and 1. Doubling every element, to get [2 2; 0 2], is 2A, not A².

questions.stem: A stall sells pies at $3, sausage rolls at $5 and drinks at $2. It sells 10 pies, 4 sausage rolls and 6 drinks. The product [3 5 2] × [10; 4; 6] gives the total takings, which are:
questions.explanation: The row matrix of prices times the column matrix of quantities is 3 × 10 + 5 × 4 + 2 × 6 = 30 + 20 + 12 = $62. Adding the prices and the quantities separately gives meaningless totals.

questions.stem: P = [0 1 0; 0 0 1; 1 0 0] (rows separated by semicolons). The product P × [A; B; C] is:
options: [C; A; B]
[A; B; C]
[B; A; C]
[B; C; A]
questions.explanation: Row 1 of P picks the second element, row 2 picks the third and row 3 picks the first, giving B, C, A. A permutation matrix only rearranges the elements.

questions.stem: In the square of a communication matrix, C², the element in row 1, column 3 is 2. This means that person 1 can send a message to person 3:
options: in two ways, each through exactly one other person
directly, in two different ways
in two ways, each through exactly two other people
in one way, through exactly two other people
questions.explanation: C² counts two-step links, so there are two different routes from person 1 to person 3 that pass through one intermediary. Direct links are counted in C itself.

questions.stem: In a dominance matrix D for a round-robin tournament, the row sums of D give:
options: the total number of matches played by everyone
the number of one-step dominances of each player
the number of matches lost by each player
the number of two-step dominances of each player
questions.explanation: A 1 in row X, column Y shows X defeated Y, so each row sum counts a player’s direct wins, the one-step dominances. Two-step dominances are given by the row sums of D².

questions.stem: Of the people who shop at store X this week, 90% shop at X next week and the rest go to Y. Of those at Y, 40% move to X. With columns as this week (X, Y), the transition matrix is:
questions.explanation: Column X holds 0.9 staying and 0.1 leaving; column Y holds 0.4 moving to X and 0.6 staying. Writing the X proportions across a row gives [0.9 0.1; 0.4 0.6], whose columns do not add to 1.

questions.stem: T = [0.9 0.4; 0.1 0.6] and S(0) = [500; 500] (rows separated by semicolons). Using S(n + 1) = T × S(n), the state matrix S(1) is:
In the transition matrix T = [0.7 0.4; 0.3 0.6], with columns as this week and rows as next week (states X, Y), the element 0.3 means that:
options: 30% of those in Y this week are in X next week
30% of those in X this week stay in X next week
30% of everyone is in Y next week
30% of those in X this week are in Y next week
questions.explanation: The element sits in column X (this week) and row Y (next week), so it is the proportion moving from X to Y. The move from Y to X is the 0.4 in row X, column Y.

questions.stem: An insect population is modelled by S(n + 1) = L × S(n), with L = [0 0 20; 0.1 0 0; 0 0.5 0] and S(0) = [1000; 200; 50] for eggs, juveniles and adults. After one step, the number of adults is:
questions.explanation: Row 3 of L gives adults = 0.5 × juveniles = 0.5 × 200 = 100. Applying 0.5 to the 50 current adults, to get 25, uses the wrong age group.

questions.stem: In a Leslie matrix, the element 0.5 in row 3, column 2 represents:
options: the proportion of age group 2 that dies before the next step
the proportion of age group 2 that survives into age group 3
the number of offspring born to each member of age group 3
the proportion of age group 3 that survives into age group 2
questions.explanation: Below the top row, a Leslie matrix holds survival rates: column 2 is the current age group and row 3 is the next. Birth rates are in the top row.

questions.stem: A population is modelled by S(n + 1) = T × S(n) + B, where S lists three regions and B = [0; 50; −20]. The matrix B shows that, each step:
options: region 1 is restocked with 30 and region 3 is culled
50 are added to region 2 and 20 are removed from region 3
50 are removed from region 2 and 20 are added to region 3
50% of region 2 and 20% of region 3 are culled
questions.explanation: B is added after the transitions: +50 restocks region 2, −20 culls region 3, and 0 leaves region 1 unchanged. B holds numbers, not percentages.

questions.stem: The transpose of the matrix [1 2 3; 4 5 6] (rows separated by semicolons) is:
questions.explanation: Transposing turns each row into a column, so the 2 × 3 matrix becomes 3 × 2 with rows 1 4, 2 5 and 3 6. Swapping the order of the rows is not a transpose.

questions.stem: For two 2 × 2 matrices A and B, which statement is true in general?
options: AB and BA may be different
AB always equals BA
AB is defined but BA is not
AB always equals A + B
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: rows of the first matrix are combined with columns of the second, so swapping the order usually changes the result. Both products exist for square matrices of the same order.

questions.stem: A transition matrix with columns adding to 1 models the movement of a fixed population. After many steps, the total population:
options: grows by the same amount each step
falls to zero
doubles at each step
stays the same as at the start
questions.explanation: Because each column adds to 1, everyone in each state is redistributed but nobody is added or lost. Only culling, restocking or births would change the total.

questions.stem: A shop’s monthly sales are stored in a matrix with rows for branches and columns for products. The element in row 2, column 3 gives:
options: the total sales at branch 2
the total sales of product 3
the sales of product 3 at branch 2
the sales of product 2 at branch 3
questions.explanation: An element is named by its row then its column, so row 2 (branch 2) and column 3 (product 3). Totals would come from row or column sums.

questions.stem: In a round-robin, A defeated B and C, B defeated C and D, C defeated D, and D defeated A. Ranking by one-step plus two-step dominances, the order from first to last is:
options: A, B, D, C
A, B, C, D
B, A, D, C
A, D, B, C
questions.explanation: One-step wins: A 2, B 2, C 1, D 1. Two-step: A 3, B 2, C 1, D 2. Totals: A 5, B 4, D 3, C 2. Using wins alone cannot separate A from B or C from D.

questions.stem: T = [0.7 0.2; 0.3 0.8] models 1000 shoppers moving between stores X and Y (columns as this week, rows as next week). In the long run, the number shopping at X settles at about:
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the flow from X to Y equals the flow back: 0.3x = 0.2y, so x : y = 2 : 3, giving 400 at X and 600 at Y. 600 swaps the ratio.

questions.stem: T = [0.9 0.2; 0.1 0.8] and S(0) = [100; 100] (rows separated by semicolons). Using S(n + 1) = T × S(n), the state matrix S(2) is:
T = [0.9 0.2; 0.1 0.8], S(0) = [200; 100] and B = [10; −10] (rows separated by semicolons). Using S(n + 1) = T × S(n) + B, the state matrix S(1) is:
questions.explanation: T × S(0) = [180 + 20; 20 + 80] = [200; 100], and adding B gives [210; 90]. [190; 110] subtracts B instead of adding it.

questions.stem: Which of these transition matrices is not regular (rows separated by semicolons)?
questions.explanation: Powers of [0 1; 1 0] alternate between itself and the identity, so a zero element always remains and the states swap forever. [0 0.4; 1 0.6] has a zero, but its square has all positive elements.

questions.stem: The simultaneous equations 2x + y = 5 and x + y = 3 are written as [2 1; 1 1] × [x; y] = [5; 3]. Using the inverse matrix [1 −1; −1 2], the solution is:
questions.explanation: [x; y] = [1 −1; −1 2] × [5; 3] = [5 − 3; −5 + 6] = [2; 1]. Check: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 and 2 + 1 = 3. The inverse must multiply on the left of the constants.

questions.stem: A = [2 6; 1 3] (rows separated by semicolons). Which statement is true?
options: A has no inverse, because its determinant is 0
A has an inverse, because it has no zero elements
A has no inverse, because it is not symmetric
A has an inverse, because its determinant is 12
questions.explanation: det A = 2 × 3 − 6 × 1 = 0, so A is singular and has no inverse. A matrix with no zero elements can still have a zero determinant.

questions.stem: A binary matrix F records friendships among four students, with F = F transposed. This tells us that:
options: every student is friends with every other student
no student is friends with any other student
the number of friendships is a perfect square
every friendship is recorded in both directions
questions.explanation: F equal to its transpose means F is symmetric: if row X, column Y is 1 then row Y, column X is also 1, so friendship goes both ways. It says nothing about how many friendships exist.

questions.stem: A Leslie matrix model gives S(n + 1) = L × S(n). Unlike a transition matrix model, the total population:
options: can change, because births are added and not all individuals survive
stays fixed, because each column of L must add to 1
can only fall, because survival rates are below 1
can only rise, because birth rates are positive
questions.explanation: The columns of a Leslie matrix need not add to 1: births add individuals and survival rates below 1 remove them, so the total can grow or shrink. A transition matrix keeps a fixed population.

questions.stem: A communication matrix C has zeros on its leading diagonal and is not symmetric. This means that:
options: every link between two people works in both directions
each person sends only to themselves
no one sends to themselves, and some links are one-way
everyone can send directly to everyone else
questions.explanation: Zeros on the diagonal show no one communicates with themselves. If C were symmetric, every link would be two-way; since it is not, at least one link works in one direction only.
